html:
Potential of two charged spheres
Height = electric potential V(x,y). Hill = positive sphere (right), well = negative sphere (left). Both tips are cut flat where the conducting sphere surface begins.
Representation
Equally spaced levels: solid above V = 0, dashed below. Crowded rings = steep surface = strong field.
Guided tour
Hover the surface to read V at a point.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional surface plot enclosed in a thin rectangular wireframe box, with no axis labels, tick marks, or numerical scales shown. A broad flat blue sheet spans the box at mid-height, standing for the level far from the charges. On the right half of the sheet the surface rises into a steep, narrow peak whose flanks are banded in pink and violet and whose tip is cut off flat. On the left half the surface plunges into a matching funnel-shaped depression, shaded the same way and likewise truncated at its base. Dark contour lines run across the surface as closed loops encircling both the peak and the pit, crowding together where the surface steepens and spreading into wide rounded loops out on the flat sheet, with a faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features. Rendering potential as height converts the sign and size of the potential into visible relief, so the hill and the trough can be read against each other directly. The plot builds intuition for the potential of two equal and opposite charges carried on conducting spheres of finite radius.

elements: thin rectangular wireframe bounding box enclosing the whole plot (no tick marks, no axis labels, no numbers)
broad flat light-blue sheet spanning the full box footprint at mid-height, representing V = 0 far from the charges
steep narrow funnel-shaped peak rising from the RIGHT half of the sheet (positive charge)
matching funnel-shaped depression plunging below the sheet on the LEFT half (negative charge)
flat circular truncation cap cutting off the tip of the peak (sphere-surface clipping)
flat circular truncation floor cutting off the bottom of the pit at the same depth
height-mapped color banding on the funnel flanks: pale blue on the flat sheet grading to pink then violet near the extremes
dark closed contour lines drawn on the surface, forming tight concentric rings on the steep flanks of both funnels
wide rounded contour loops spreading out across the flat sheet away from the charges
faint straight line crossing the flat sheet between the peak and the pit (the V = 0 symmetry line / midplane trace)
vertical wireframe box corner edges visible in front of and behind the surface

interactions.teaches: The hill and the trough are two halves of one continuous potential surface; rotating shows the pit is as deep as the peak is tall and that both decay smoothly into the flat far-field sheet.

interactions.label: Charge balance  q₋ / q₊
interactions.teaches: Potential is a signed scalar: the sign of each charge decides whether the surface rises or falls, and the magnitude sets how tall the peak or how deep the well is. At -1 the figure is perfectly antisymmetric; away from -1 the flat sheet tilts because the net charge no longer cancels.

interactions.label: Charge separation d
interactions.teaches: As the equal and opposite charges are brought together the hill and trough overlap and partially cancel, flattening the region between them; pulled apart, each funnel becomes an isolated point-charge potential with its own concentric contours.

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: Contour loops are just the level curves of the height surface: where the surface is steep the contours crowd together, and crowded contours mean a large potential gradient, i.e. a strong electric field.
Reading a single point off the surface gives the local potential value and shows how it falls as 1/r from each sphere, with the superposed value being the simple sum of the two contributions.

demo_steps.title: Equal and opposite charges
demo_steps.narration: A single smooth surface: potential rises into a steep peak over the positive sphere on the right and drops into an identical well over the negative sphere on the left, flattening to zero far away.

demo_steps.title: Contours read the slope
demo_steps.narration: Adding level curves shows the loops packed tightly on the steep flanks and spread wide out on the flat sheet — close contours mark a strong field, wide ones a weak field.

demo_steps.title: Flatten to the contour map
demo_steps.narration: Looking straight down, the relief collapses into the familiar equipotential map: nested loops around each sphere and a straight zero-potential line down the middle.

demo_steps.title: Unbalance the charges
demo_steps.narration: Weakening the negative charge shrinks its well and lifts the far-field sheet above zero — the net charge no longer cancels, and the zero line bends around the smaller charge.

demo_steps.title: Bring them together
demo_steps.narration: Sliding the spheres close, the peak and well overlap and largely cancel, leaving a compact dipole with a fast-collapsing potential and contours that close in tightly around the pair.

demo_steps.title: Pull them apart
demo_steps.narration: Widely separated, each funnel becomes an essentially isolated point-charge potential with its own circular contours, and the region between goes nearly flat.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Domain: x ∈ [-3, 3] (screen-right), y ∈ [-3, 3] (receding depth), V plotted on the vertical axis z ∈ [-1.5, 1.5]. Bounding wireframe box is therefore 6 × 6 × 3 world units, drawn as thin gray (#909090) lines, ~1px, with the box wider than tall as in the source (roughly 1.6:1 screen aspect). The flat V = 0 sheet sits exactly at box mid-height, spanning the full 6 × 6 footprint. Potential: V(x,y) = k[ q₊ / max(r₊, a) + q₋ / max(r₋, a) ] with k = 1, q₊ = +1, q₋ = chargeBalance × 1, sphere radius a = 0.32, r± = sqrt((x ∓ d/2)² + y²). Charges sit on the x-axis at (+d/2, 0) POSITIVE = right-hand peak and (−d/2, 0) NEGATIVE = left-hand pit, with default d = 2.5 (so +1.25 and −1.25). Surface is hard-clipped at z = ±1.5, producing the flat circular cap on the peak tip and the flat circular floor in the pit, both ~0.5 units across — these truncations are visible in the source and must be kept. Left funnel in the source reads slightly smaller/further away than the right peak purely because of the viewing angle; keep them mathematically identical. Colors sampled from source: flat sheet / low relief light cornflower blue #8FC0EA to #A9D4F5; mid-flank pink #EFA6C8; steepest near-tip violet/purple #9C6FD2 to #7F5BC0; contour lines near-black #1A1A28 at ~0.8px, drawn as level sets of V at even spacing (about 12–16 levels over the full range) so they naturally crowd on the flanks; wireframe box #8A8A8A; background white. The faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features is the V = 0 trace at x = 0 (plus the box's mid grid line) — draw it as a thin ~#6E7EA0 line running along the depth direction. Grid the surface at least 160 × 160 so the funnel walls stay smooth.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the surface as a single indexed BufferGeometry over the (x,y) grid with per-vertex color from a height ramp (blue → pink → violet), MeshLambert/MeshStandard with flatShading off, side = DoubleSide so the pit interior reads correctly. Clamp z to ±1.5 per vertex, which automatically yields the flat truncation caps; optionally add explicit circular disks at the clip planes so the caps are opaque. Contours: compute marching-squares polylines on the same scalar grid per frame and render as LineSegments offset ~0.005 along the surface normal (or use polygonOffset) to avoid z-fighting. For the top-down contour mode, tween the camera to elevation 90° and tween all z-values toward 0 rather than swapping objects, so the learner sees the relief flatten into the loops. Regenerate vertex positions/colors in place when either slider changes — do not rebuild geometry. Box is a LineSegments wireframe, no ticks or labels. Soft directional key light from upper-left plus ambient so the violet flanks stay readable; no shadows.

authoredContext:
To improve your intuition, we show a three-dimensional variant of the potential in a system with two opposing charges. The figure displays a three-dimensional map of electric potential, where lines on the map are for equipotential surfaces. The hill is at the positive charge, and the trough is at the negative charge. The potential is zero far away from the charges. Note that the cut off at a particular potential implies that the charges are on conducting spheres with a finite radius.

Electric potential map of two opposite charges of equal magnitude on conducting spheres. The potential is negative near the negative charge and positive near the positive charge.

The illustration shows electric potential map and equipotential lines two charges – one positive and one negative.

A two-dimensional map of the cross-sectional plane that contains both charges is shown in the figure. The line that is equidistant from the two opposite charges corresponds to zero potential, since at the points on the line, the positive potential from the positive charge cancels the negative potential from the negative charge. Equipotential lines in the cross-sectional plane are closed loops, which are not necessarily circles, since at each point, the net potential is the sum of the potentials from each charge.

discrepancies: The peak and well are noticeably narrower/steeper than in the source: in the original each funnel spreads over roughly a third of the plate with a broad flared skirt, while the generated hill/pit are compact cones occupying a small fraction of the sheet, so the surface reads as two spikes on a large flat plane.

Contour density and extent differ: the source shows many nested level curves that spread far out over the flat blue sheet (including large loops encircling each charge), whereas the generated figure draws only a handful of tight rings close to each extremum, leaving most of the sheet bare.

The '+q' label does not appear at the peak in the rendered view, and the '−q' label floats near the middle of the plate rather than clearly attached to the well, making the two annotations asymmetric and ambiguous.
Small red/blue charge-marker spheres are added at the peak/pit apexes; these do not exist in the source figure and slightly clutter the apex caps.
Surface colour is duller than the source — the flat sheet is a desaturated grey-blue and the peak's pink→violet ramp is less vivid than the strongly saturated pink/violet gradient in the original.
evaluation.notes: A correct and well-built 3D potential surface with box frame, V=0 sheet, contours and a rich set of meaningful controls (charge balance, separation, representation modes, guided tour, hover probe); main weaknesses are the over-compact peak/well profiles, sparse contours compared with the source, and weak/ambiguous +q / −q labelling.
action_items: Widen the funnels: reduce the clamp VCLAMP or increase K/A so each peak and well flares over a visibly larger patch of the plate, matching the broad skirts in the source.
Add more contour levels (finer spacing near V≈0) so level curves extend across the flat sheet as large loops, as in the original, and consider dashed styling for the hidden portions.
Fix label placement: anchor '+q' just above the clipped peak cap and '−q' just below the well bottom with a leader offset so both are visible and unambiguous; bump font size for readability.
Boost the colour saturation of the sheet and the pink/violet ramp to match the source's vivid gradient, and consider removing or shrinking the added charge-marker spheres.

interactions.teaches: The hill and the trough are two halves of one continuous potential surface; rotating shows the pit is as deep as the peak is tall and that both decay smoothly into the flat far-field sheet.

interactions.label: Charge balance  q₋ / q₊
interactions.teaches: Potential is a signed scalar: the sign of each charge decides whether the surface rises or falls, and the magnitude sets how tall the peak or how deep the well is. At -1 the figure is perfectly antisymmetric; away from -1 the flat sheet tilts because the net charge no longer cancels.

interactions.label: Charge separation d
interactions.teaches: As the equal and opposite charges are brought together the hill and trough overlap and partially cancel, flattening the region between them; pulled apart, each funnel becomes an isolated point-charge potential with its own concentric contours.

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: Contour loops are just the level curves of the height surface: where the surface is steep the contours crowd together, and crowded contours mean a large potential gradient, i.e. a strong electric field.
Reading a single point off the surface gives the local potential value and shows how it falls as 1/r from each sphere, with the superposed value being the simple sum of the two contributions.

demo_steps.title: Equal and opposite charges
demo_steps.narration: A single smooth surface: potential rises into a steep peak over the positive sphere on the right and drops into an identical well over the negative sphere on the left, flattening to zero far away.

demo_steps.title: Contours read the slope
demo_steps.narration: Adding level curves shows the loops packed tightly on the steep flanks and spread wide out on the flat sheet — close contours mark a strong field, wide ones a weak field.

demo_steps.title: Flatten to the contour map
demo_steps.narration: Looking straight down, the relief collapses into the familiar equipotential map: nested loops around each sphere and a straight zero-potential line down the middle.

demo_steps.title: Unbalance the charges
demo_steps.narration: Weakening the negative charge shrinks its well and lifts the far-field sheet above zero — the net charge no longer cancels, and the zero line bends around the smaller charge.

demo_steps.title: Bring them together
demo_steps.narration: Sliding the spheres close, the peak and well overlap and largely cancel, leaving a compact dipole with a fast-collapsing potential and contours that close in tightly around the pair.

demo_steps.title: Pull them apart
demo_steps.narration: Widely separated, each funnel becomes an essentially isolated point-charge potential with its own circular contours, and the region between goes nearly flat.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Domain: x ∈ [-3, 3] (screen-right), y ∈ [-3, 3] (receding depth), V plotted on the vertical axis z ∈ [-1.5, 1.5]. Bounding wireframe box is therefore 6 × 6 × 3 world units, drawn as thin gray (#909090) lines, ~1px, with the box wider than tall as in the source (roughly 1.6:1 screen aspect). The flat V = 0 sheet sits exactly at box mid-height, spanning the full 6 × 6 footprint. Potential: V(x,y) = k[ q₊ / max(r₊, a) + q₋ / max(r₋, a) ] with k = 1, q₊ = +1, q₋ = chargeBalance × 1, sphere radius a = 0.32, r± = sqrt((x ∓ d/2)² + y²). Charges sit on the x-axis at (+d/2, 0) POSITIVE = right-hand peak and (−d/2, 0) NEGATIVE = left-hand pit, with default d = 2.5 (so +1.25 and −1.25). Surface is hard-clipped at z = ±1.5, producing the flat circular cap on the peak tip and the flat circular floor in the pit, both ~0.5 units across — these truncations are visible in the source and must be kept. Left funnel in the source reads slightly smaller/further away than the right peak purely because of the viewing angle; keep them mathematically identical. Colors sampled from source: flat sheet / low relief light cornflower blue #8FC0EA to #A9D4F5; mid-flank pink #EFA6C8; steepest near-tip violet/purple #9C6FD2 to #7F5BC0; contour lines near-black #1A1A28 at ~0.8px, drawn as level sets of V at even spacing (about 12–16 levels over the full range) so they naturally crowd on the flanks; wireframe box #8A8A8A; background white. The faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features is the V = 0 trace at x = 0 (plus the box's mid grid line) — draw it as a thin ~#6E7EA0 line running along the depth direction. Grid the surface at least 160 × 160 so the funnel walls stay smooth.
